stages.title: Materials & Surfaces
stages.description: What separates watercolor, gouache, acrylic and oil paint, and how to choose and prepare brushes, paper and canvas for each.
learningObjectives: Name the binder of watercolor, gouache, acrylic and oil paint and how each dries
Explain opacity and rewettability differences between watercolor, gouache and acrylic
Choose a suitable brush type and cleanup solvent for acrylic versus oil
Prepare a support correctly: sizing/priming canvas and selecting watercolor paper weight and surface

explainBack.question: You are setting up to paint in watercolor, gouache, acrylic and oil. For each, what holds the pigment, how does it dry, and how would you prepare the paper or canvas?
rubric: Watercolor and gouache both use gum arabic as binder and stay rewettable when dry; watercolor is transparent, gouache is opaque and matte
Acrylic is pigment in a polymer binder: water-soluble while wet, dries fast (about an hour) and becomes water-resistant; it looks lighter wet than dry
Oil paint is pigment in a drying oil (linseed is most common) that forms a film on exposure to air; it dries slowly and is thinned/cleaned with mineral spirits or turpentine
Raw canvas must be sized/primed before oil; acrylic gesso needs no sizing and accepts both acrylic and oil, but acrylic should not go over an oil ground
Watercolor paper comes as hot-pressed (smooth), cold-pressed/NOT (medium) and rough; sheets lighter than about 356 gsm (260 lb), such as 300 gsm/140 lb, should be stretched to avoid warping

resources.title: What is the difference between oil paint, acrylic paint, watercolour paint, and gouache?
resources.description: A side-by-side introduction to the four common paint types and how they behave on the page.
keyPoints: Compares oil, acrylic, watercolour and gouache
Covers how each paint type handles and dries
Aimed at beginners choosing a first medium

resources.title: Gouache vs. Watercolor: What's the Difference?
resources.description: Explains why gouache is opaque and matte while watercolor is transparent, though both use gum arabic.
keyPoints: Both traditionally bound with gum arabic
Gouache has a higher pigment load, often with chalk or white as opacifier
Watercolor is transparent and dries lighter than it looks wet
Both stay rewettable after drying, unlike acrylic

resources.title: Notes on Acrylic Painting
resources.description: University studio notes on how acrylic behaves, which brushes to use and how to thin it.
keyPoints: Pigment in a polymer binder that dissolves in water until dry
Dries in about an hour; tools wash with soap and water
Binder is milky when wet, so colors look lighter wet than dry
Use synthetic brushes; natural bristles swell and break down

resources.title: Oil paint
resources.description: Museum glossary entry defining oil paint and explaining why it dries slowly.
keyPoints: Pigment suspended in a drying oil that forms a tough film in air
Linseed is the most used oil; poppy, safflower and walnut also used
Thin layers diluted with turpentine dry in days; oil-rich layers harden over years

resources.title: Preparation of the Painting Ground
resources.description: How to size and prime canvas or panel, and when acrylic gesso can be used.
keyPoints: Oil in direct contact with canvas causes deterioration, so size first
Traditional route: rabbitskin glue size then oil ground
Acrylic gesso needs no sizing and takes both acrylic and oil
Acrylic paint will not go over an oil surface

resources.title: Watercolour Paper
resources.provider: UCL Slade School of Fine Art
resources.description: Art-school materials note on watercolour paper weights, surfaces and when to stretch paper.
keyPoints: Common weights: 190 gsm (90 lb), 300 gsm (140 lb), 356 gsm (260 lb), 638 gsm (300 lb)
Paper under 356 gsm should be stretched or it is likely to warp
Surfaces: rough, hot-pressed (smooth) and cold-pressed/NOT (in between)
Acid-free papers yellow less over time

stages.title: Drawing Fundamentals: Line & Proportion
stages.description: Using line and simple shapes, and measuring by sighting, to draw what you see in correct proportion.
learningObjectives: Sight and measure proportions with a pencil held at arm's length
Check angles and alignments with sighted angles and plumb/organizational lines
Block in a subject big-to-small using simple enclosing shapes
Use contour, cross-contour and line weight deliberately

explainBack.question: Describe how you would measure and block in a still life so its proportions are accurate, and how you would then use line to describe it.
rubric: Sighting: hold the pencil at arm's length with the elbow locked and one eye closed so the measuring distance stays constant
Pick one part as a unit (marked with the thumb on the pencil) and compare other heights and widths as multiples of it
Angles are sighted by matching the pencil to an edge and transferring that angle; plumb (vertical) and horizontal lines check alignments
Work big to small: enclose the subject in a simple proportioned shape or box, then subdivide before adding detail
Contour lines describe edges, cross-contour lines travel across a form to show volume, and heavier line weight tends to read as nearer

resources.title: Drawing Measuring Techniques
resources.description: Stan Prokopenko demonstrates several ways to measure proportions while drawing from observation.
keyPoints: Pencil sighting at arm's length
Using a unit to compare sizes
Checking alignments and angles

resources.title: How to Draw Accurate Proportions
resources.description: Free lesson page summarising sighting, plumb lines, angles, units and big-to-small block-in.
keyPoints: Locked elbow, one eye closed, pencil tip and thumb mark a unit
Plumb lines find vertical/horizontal alignments
Angles relate any two points, not just aligned ones
Start with the envelope, then break into smaller shapes; check negative shapes

resources.title: Observation
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on sighting, angle measurement, plumb/axis lines and the proportion box.
keyPoints: Sighting tool at arm's length, locked elbow, one eye closed
Thumb marks a unit for comparing height, width and spacing
Match pencil to an edge to read its angle
Proportion box: ratio of height to width sets the starting rectangle

resources.title: Line
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on kinds of line and how line weight communicates space and surface.
keyPoints: Contour, blind contour and modified contour lines
Cross-contour lines run across a form to show volume
Heavier lines tend to come forward, lighter lines recede

stages.title: Value, Light & Shadow
stages.description: Reading and rendering light on form with a value scale and the standard light and shadow zones.
learningObjectives: Build a step value scale from white to black
Explain how a plane's angle to the light sets its value
Identify highlight, light, halftone, terminator/core shadow, reflected light, form shadow and cast shadow

explainBack.question: A white ball sits on a table under one lamp. Name the light and shadow areas you would render and explain what causes each.
rubric: A value scale runs from white to black in steps (a common scale has nine values) or as a smooth gradient
Value depends on plane orientation: planes facing the light are lightest and planes turned further away receive less light and get darker
Form shadow is on the object where planes turn away from the light; cast shadow is where the object blocks light from another surface
The core shadow is the darker band along the terminator; reflected light bounced from nearby surfaces lightens the shadow side
The highlight is a reflection of the light source and shifts with the viewer's position, distinct from the plane facing the light

resources.title: Shading Light and Form - Basics
resources.description: Introductory lesson naming the zones of light and shadow on simple forms.
keyPoints: Terminator divides light from shadow
Form shadow vs cast shadow
Core shadow, reflected light and highlight

resources.title: Shading Light and Form – Basics
resources.description: Lesson notes defining each light and shadow zone with short explanations.
keyPoints: Form shadow: planes turned away from the light
Cast shadow: one form blocks light from another
Core shadow: darker band along the terminator
Highlight is a reflection of the source and moves with the viewer

resources.title: Value
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on value scales, the parts of light on form, hatching and chiaroscuro.
keyPoints: Standard nine-step scale from white to black
Step scales vs gradient scales
Highlight, light, core shadow, reflected light, cast and form shadow
Hatching and cross-hatching build value

resources.title: Grayscale and Planar Changes in Value
resources.description: Explains how value changes as planes turn relative to the light source.
keyPoints: A plane at 45 degrees to the light gets less light than one facing it
Even white objects contain many grays
Background value changes how the object's value is read

stages.title: Perspective
stages.description: Creating depth with linear perspective (one-, two- and three-point) and atmospheric perspective.
learningObjectives: Place a horizon line at eye level and locate vanishing points on it
Choose between one-, two- and three-point perspective for a given view
Apply atmospheric perspective to push distant forms back

explainBack.question: Explain how you would draw a box seen straight on, a building seen from its corner, and a skyscraper seen from the street, then make distant hills recede.
rubric: The horizon line is the viewer's eye level; vanishing points sit on it and receding parallel lines (orthogonals) converge to them
One-point: one vanishing point, used when the object's faces are parallel/perpendicular to the viewer (head-on)
Two-point: used when looking at an object's corner; two vanishing points on the horizon, and verticals stay at 90 degrees to the horizon
Three-point adds a third vanishing point above the horizon (worm's-eye) or below it (bird's-eye), so verticals also converge
Atmospheric perspective: distant objects show less contrast, detail and saturation and shift toward a bluer gray

resources.title: Two-Point Perspective Drawing Made Simple
resources.description: Walkthrough of setting up a horizon and two vanishing points and building boxes in two-point perspective.
keyPoints: Horizon line and two vanishing points
Constructing boxes seen from a corner
Keeping verticals vertical

resources.title: Perspective
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on horizon line, vanishing points and the three linear perspective systems.
keyPoints: Horizon line = eye level
Orthogonals converge to vanishing points
One-, two- and three-point systems compared
Overlap, scale and atmospheric perspective add depth

resources.title: Introduction to Linear Perspective
resources.description: Defines horizon line, vanishing point and convergence lines for one-point perspective.
keyPoints: Horizon line always stays at your eye level
Receding parallels meet at the vanishing point
One-point needs planes parallel or perpendicular to you

resources.title: Exteriors (Two Point)
resources.description: How to find the two vanishing points when viewing an object's corner.
keyPoints: Use two-point when looking at an object's corner
Verticals are 90 degrees to the horizon in one- and two-point
Vanishing points may fall outside the picture

resources.title: Three-Point Perspective
resources.description: Explains the third vanishing point for worm's-eye and bird's-eye views.
keyPoints: Third VP above the horizon for worm's-eye views
Third VP below the horizon for bird's-eye views
Used for extreme heights such as tall buildings

resources.title: Depth and Atmosphere (Aerial Perspective)
resources.description: How atmosphere changes contrast, color and detail with distance.
keyPoints: Contrast and detail drop with distance
Whites and blacks drift toward a bluer gray
Saturation decreases with distance

stages.title: Color Theory & Mixing
stages.description: Describing color by hue, value and saturation, and using the color wheel, complements and temperature to mix paint.
learningObjectives: Describe any color by hue, value and saturation (chroma)
Use the color wheel to find complements and explain what mixing them does
Explain why mixtures lose intensity and how to keep mixes clean
Treat color temperature as relative and set up warm and cool primaries

explainBack.question: Your mixed green looks dull and a red area looks too loud. Using hue, value, saturation, complements and temperature, explain what is happening and how you would fix each.
rubric: Hue is the color name, value is its lightness or darkness, and saturation/chroma is its intensity
Complements sit opposite each other on the color wheel; mixing a color with its complement neutralizes (lowers the saturation of) it
Every pigment mix loses intensity, so a pure pigment (e.g. a tube green) is more saturated than a blue-yellow mix
Adding white (tint) or black (shade) changes value; a tone can match a hue's value while being less vivid
Color temperature is relative (a blue can read warm or cool next to another blue); a practical palette has a warm and a cool version of each primary

resources.title: Color Theory Basics for Digital Painters
resources.description: Marco Bucci explains hue, saturation and value as the three properties of any color.
keyPoints: Hue is the name of the color
Saturation is intensity
Value is lightness and carries form

resources.title: Learning Color Temperature Will Change How You Paint
resources.description: Lesson on warm and cool color and how temperature shifts are used in painting.
keyPoints: What makes a color warm or cool
Temperature as a relationship
Using temperature shifts in light and shadow

resources.title: Color
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on color properties, the 12-hue wheel, temperature and color schemes.
keyPoints: Hue, value and saturation defined
Primary, secondary and tertiary hues on a 12-part wheel
Complements neutralize each other when mixed
Analogous, triadic and monochromatic schemes

resources.title: The Color Wheel and Color Complements
resources.description: Explains primaries, secondaries and complementary pairs, including how complements interact side by side.
keyPoints: Complements sit opposite and contrast most strongly
Itten's balancing ratios for complement pairs
Adjacent complements can appear to vibrate

resources.title: Color Chroma and Intensity
resources.description: Explains chroma versus value and why mixtures lose intensity.
keyPoints: The pure hue has the highest chroma
Tints add white, shades add black
Mixing pigments lowers intensity; buy pure green for max saturation

resources.title: Understanding warm and cool colours
resources.description: Manufacturer guide arguing color temperature is relative and recommending warm and cool primaries.
keyPoints: No fixed warm/cool list; temperature depends on neighbors
Closer to red reads warmer, closer to green cooler
Choose the warmest and coolest version of each primary
Paint your own wheel to learn your colors

stages.title: Composition & Value Planning
stages.description: Arranging a picture with a clear focal point, balance and eye movement, planned through small notan thumbnails.
learningObjectives: Place focal points using the rule of thirds
Create emphasis and guide the eye with contrast, placement and line
Balance a picture asymmetrically
Plan value structure with small two- or three-value notan thumbnails

explainBack.question: Before painting a landscape, how would you plan its composition so the viewer looks where you want and the design holds together?
rubric: Rule of thirds: two horizontal and two vertical lines divide the picture into nine parts; key elements go on the lines or their four intersections rather than the center
A focal point is created through emphasis such as the strongest contrast, color, lighting or placement
Diagonal and directional lines imply movement and lead the eye through the picture
Asymmetrical balance offsets visual weight, e.g. one large dark shape balancing several smaller ones
Notan thumbnails simplify the scene into two (or three) values in small sketches that design big shapes without detail

resources.title: Using Notan Sketches to Strengthen Composition
resources.description: Painter demonstrates simplifying a scene into light and dark notan sketches before painting.
keyPoints: What a notan sketch is
Reducing a reference to big light and dark shapes
Using the sketch to plan a painting

resources.title: Learning Activity: The Rule of Thirds
resources.description: Museum activity explaining the rule of thirds grid with an O'Keeffe example.
keyPoints: Four lines divide the picture into nine equal sections
The four intersections are visual hot spots
Placing subjects off-center draws the eye into the work

resources.title: Elements of Art & Principles of Design
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on balance, emphasis, movement, unity, variety, contrast and scale.
keyPoints: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance
Emphasis via color, lighting, placement or contrast
Diagonal and radiating lines imply movement
Unity and variety work together

resources.title: General Compositional Layout
resources.description: Short guide to asymmetrical balance and leading the viewer's eye.
keyPoints: Good compositions are often asymmetrical or lead the eye around
One heavy shape can balance several light ones
Vary size and value rather than repeating identical areas

resources.title: Project - Notan Master Thumbnails
resources.description: Assignment page explaining notan and how to make small value thumbnails.
keyPoints: Notan: sort everything into lights or darks around a threshold
Optionally add a mid-tone for 3 values
Keep thumbnails small to avoid detail
Design large shapes and assign each a value

stages.title: Painting Techniques & Layering
stages.description: Building paintings in sound layers: oil layering rules, glazing, impasto and watercolor wet-on-wet versus wet-on-dry.
learningObjectives: Apply fat over lean, thick over thin and slow-drying over fast-drying in oil
Distinguish a glaze from a scumble and use impasto deliberately
Choose wet-on-wet or wet-on-dry watercolor for the edge you want
Layer watercolor washes light to dark and correct by lifting

explainBack.question: Explain how you would layer an oil painting so it will not crack, and how you would get both soft and crisp edges in a watercolor.
rubric: Fat over lean: each oil layer has more oil/medium than the one beneath, so upper layers are more flexible and less likely to crack
Thick over thin and slow-drying over fast-drying: thin, fast-drying paint goes underneath; impasto and slow-drying colors go last
A glaze is a transparent film over a lighter layer that modifies its color; a thin layer lighter than what is beneath is a scumble; impasto is thick paint showing brush or knife marks
Wet-on-wet (paint into wet paper) gives soft, diffused edges and dilutes color, so mix darker; wet-on-dry gives crisp, controlled edges
Watercolor is built light to dark, letting each wash dry before the next; a damp brush can lift dried paint to lighten or soften

resources.title: Wet-On-Wet Watercolour Tips & Techniques: Winsor & Newton Masterclass
resources.description: Winsor & Newton masterclass demonstration of painting wet-on-wet in watercolour.
keyPoints: Wetting paper before adding color
Soft blends and diffused edges
Controlling water and timing

resources.title: What are the three oil painting rules?
resources.description: Manufacturer guide to fat over lean, thick over thin and slow-drying over fast-drying.
keyPoints: Each layer should contain more oil/medium than the one below
Fat over lean = flexible over less flexible, to prevent cracking
Thick over thin: thin layers dry faster, so they go first
Use fast-drying colors for underpainting, slow ones last

resources.title: Glaze
resources.description: Museum glossary entry defining a glaze and distinguishing it from a scumble.
keyPoints: Transparent or translucent paint film in an oil or oil-resin medium
Applied over a lighter layer to modify its color
A thin layer lighter than what is beneath is a scumble

resources.title: Impasto
resources.description: Museum glossary entry on impasto and its history.
keyPoints: An area of thick paint or texture
Brush or knife marks stay visible
Prominent from Titian and Rubens to Auerbach

resources.title: Working wet on wet in watercolour
resources.description: Demonstration article contrasting wet-on-wet with wet-on-dry watercolor.
keyPoints: Wet-on-wet: color moves and mixes on pre-wetted paper
Soft diffused edges vs sharper wet-on-dry edges
Mix tones slightly darker because water dilutes them
Some pigments separate on wet paper

resources.title: Wet Media
resources.provider: Foundations of Drawing (Palomar College, open textbook)
resources.description: Open-textbook chapter on washes, layering and lifting with water-based media.
keyPoints: Build washes from light to dark
Let each wash dry before adding another to avoid bleeding
Lift with a damp brush to lighten or soften
Cold-press paper of at least 140 lb recommended

stages.title: Studio Safety, Varnishing & Permanence
stages.description: Working safely with solvents and pigments, reading safety and lightfastness labels, and varnishing finished work.
learningObjectives: Handle solvents, oily rags and pigments safely
Read AP/CL safety seals and ASTM lightfastness ratings
Decide when and why to varnish a painting

explainBack.question: You have finished an oil painting. Describe how you clean up safely, how you check your paints will last, and when and why you would varnish it.
rubric: Oily rags can spontaneously combust: hang them flat to dry rather than leaving them crumpled
Ventilate when using solvents, wash hands, do not eat or drink while painting, and do not inhale dust when sanding pigmented layers
ACMI's AP seal marks products certified non-toxic; the CL seal marks products safe only when used as labeled (ASTM D4236)
ASTM lightfastness I (excellent) and II (very good) are suitable for lasting art; III or worse is not recommended
Varnish forms a removable protective layer that unifies sheen; apply only when paint is dry and firm in its thickest areas (weeks for Gamvar; about six months for traditional resin varnishes)

resources.title: Studio Health and Safety with Mary Tevlin from Gamblin
resources.description: Interview with a Gamblin representative about health and safety practices in the oil painting studio.
keyPoints: Safer solvent use and ventilation
Handling pigments and studio hygiene
Oily rag disposal

resources.title: Studio Safety: Create Without Compromise
resources.description: Manufacturer guide to solvent choice, ventilation, oily rags and pigment handling.
keyPoints: Hang oily rags flat to dry to avoid spontaneous combustion
Room air exchange plus open windows/fans for ventilation
Do not inhale dust when sanding cadmium or cobalt layers
Wash hands; no eating or drinking in the studio

resources.title: ACMI Seals
resources.description: Explains the AP and CL certification seals on art materials.
keyPoints: AP: toxicologist-reviewed, no materials in toxic quantities
CL: safe when used as directed with cautionary label
Smell is not a reliable guide to toxicity
Certified products conform to ASTM D4236

resources.title: How to Test for Lightfastness
resources.description: Explains ASTM lightfastness ratings and how to test a paint's fading with blue wool standards.
keyPoints: ASTM I = excellent, II = very good (about 100 years museum conditions)
Ratings worse than II are not recommended for lasting art
Blue wool scale 1-8 used as a comparison standard
Simple test: half-exposed sample in a window

resources.title: Varnishing Help
resources.description: Guide to why, when and how to varnish oil and acrylic paintings.
keyPoints: Varnish protects, unifies sheen and can be removed for conservation
Gamvar once paint is dry to the touch and firm in thickest areas
Thin work: 2-3 weeks; impasto: 1-2 months
Traditional resin varnishes need 6+ months; apply one thin coat

resources.title: Notes on Oil Painting
resources.description: University studio notes on oil handling, solvents and varnish timing.
keyPoints: Clean with mineral spirits or turpentine, or baby oil then soap
Do not varnish until six months after touch-dry
Paint keeps drying beneath the surface
